question: to the Commission Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Francesco Torselli (ECR) Subject:

Various studies and reports by customs authorities, OLAF1 and the Commission2 have highlighted instances of under-invoicing and inaccurate declarations of the value and quantity of goods imported into the European Union, particularly goods from third countries entering via major European logistics ports. Such practices can lead to the avoidance of customs duties and VAT on imports to the tune of several billion euros annually, with direct ramifications for the EU’s own resources and competition in the internal market. Given that some major European container terminals and pieces of port infrastructure are managed or part-owned by non-EU operators, including groups controlled by the Chinese state, we must ensure that checks of documents and customs requirements, as well as risk analyses on goods are uniform, rigorous throughout the logistics chain, and cannot be circumvented. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
Whether it has up-to-date estimates of the losses in customs revenue caused by underinvoicing of goods entering the EU?
Whether it considers the customs checks systems3 and risk analyses4 at Europe’s principal ports, including at terminals managed by non-EU operators, to sufficiently uniform and rigorous?
Whether it intends to shore up customs controls and anti-fraud systems to prevent the avoidance of duties and VAT on containerised imports?

OLAF (European Anti-Fraud Office) annual reports on the protection of the European Union’s financial interests and the fight against fraud, European Commission, various editions (in particular 2017–2023, which highlight cases of under-invoicing fraud in imports, with significant impact on the EU’s own resources). European Commission, annual reports on the protection of the EU’s financial interests (‘PIF’ reports): data on customs and import VAT fraud and losses amounting to billions of euros. Special Report No 19/2017 of the Court of Auditors – ‘Import procedures: shortcomings in the legal framework and an ineffective implementation impact the financial interests of the EU. Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down the Union Customs Code. This includes requirements for customs checks and risk management.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.6.2026) The Commission does not possess estimates of losses in customs revenues caused specifically by under-invoicing. Under the Union Customs Code1, customs controls are carried out by Member States’ customs authorities on the basis of risk analysis. The Commission has developed common risk criteria and standards, including for financial risks, which Member States implement in their risk-analysis systems. Under the common risk management framework, customs authorities also exchange risk information and risk-analysis results. These measures contribute to a more harmonised application of customs controls across the EU and to an equivalent level of protection, irrespective of the ports’ commercial set-up. The Commission also supports more adequate and equivalent controls through an EU funding programme supporting the purchase of customs control equipment2. Member States already use customs data and intelligence to target consignments at risk. The agreed EU Customs Reform of 26 March 20263 will further strengthen this data-driven approach through the future EU Customs Data Hub and EU Customs Authority, enhancing the EU-wide use of data analytics for risk analysis and the effectiveness of controls, thereby helping to protect the EU’s financial interests. Recent judgments4 of the Court of Justice have also clarified the legal framework for addressing undervaluation, thereby supporting the European Anti-Fraud Office and national authorities in this area.
